newsitem.title: UK: European bonds stung by Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: European bonds stung by Greenspan comments.

text.p: European bond markets tumbled through key technical support levels on Thursday, dragged down by sinking U.S. Treasuries as Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan brought inflation concerns back into the spotlight.
The June Bund future fell 22 basis points to 99.52. It recovered slightly to trade at 99.68, down 0.27 on the day by 1555 GMT.
Meanwhile the June T-bond fell through key support at 108-04, hitting a low of 107-31, before pulling back. It is currently trading at 108-07, down 8/32 on the day.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London said the key factor for European bonds would be if T-bonds closed above or below support at 107-31.
"That is the bottom of a neckline of a long-term head and shoulders on daily charts, and a close below there would confirm that we are breaking that," he said.
"If that does go, the potential target for the head and shoulders formation is five and a half points lower. So you are probably talking about a yield of seven and a quarter plus on the long bond."
Markets were spooked by Greenspan comments to a congressional hearing that the U.S. must ideally act pre-emptively to keep inflation low.
The comments heightened already rife speculation of a rise in the Fed funds rate at next Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

Beauchamp said it looked like there could potentially be a rate hike on Tuesday. "But we don't know the amount. If it is a quarter it won't be too harmful, but obviously a half will be much more so," he said.
One trader at a European bank said speculative attacks on the T-bond were trying to push the market through the key seven percent yield, onto 7.25 percent.
"They're having a go at seven and a quarter, and if that's the case we could see a point dump on the European bond markets on the back of it," he said.

"There's going to be a big punch up in the futures pit between those who want to see the market go above seven percent and those who don't. By tomorrow morning someone will have won -- we'll either be at 7.10 or 6.90 percent," he said.
